https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: The Building Canada Strong Act makes changes to federal laws to speed up the approval process for major projects, like energy and transportation infrastructure. It also updates rules for supply chains and labor relations.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary:
This bill updates several federal laws, including the Impact Assessment Act and the Canadian Energy Regulator Act, to simplify how major projects are reviewed. It sets a one-year deadline for certain decisions and allows for better coordination between government agencies and Indigenous groups during the assessment process. It also lets the government create 'regions of national interest' where projects can follow an faster approval process.

Additionally, the bill introduces new measures to strengthen Canada’s supply chains, including creating a new council to monitor trade corridors and streamlining the use of digital trade documents. It also updates labor laws under the Canada Labour Code to improve collective bargaining and payment enforcement for workers, and makes various administrative changes to marine and transportation regulations.
key_changes: It requires that certain federal impact assessments and pipeline project reviews be completed within one year.
It allows the government to designate specific regions of national interest where project approvals can be accelerated.
It establishes a National Trade Corridors Council to monitor goods movement and help prevent trade disruptions.
It enables the use of digital, electronic trade documents instead of paper ones to simplify importing and exporting.
It updates the Canada Labour Code to create new, faster processes for collective bargaining and dispute resolution.
It grants the government more power to enforce payments to workers if an employer fails to follow a settlement.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: The Canadian Fuel Affordability Act extends a tax break on fuel to help keep prices lower for Canadians until the spring of 2027.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary: This bill changes the rules for the federal excise tax, which is a specific tax added to the price of fuels like gasoline and diesel. It does this by extending a period where this tax is suspended, meaning the tax will not be charged on these fuels until January 31, 2027. This change is backdated to take effect from September 8, 2026. Following that period, the bill introduces a temporary measure for February and March 2027. During these two months, the amount of tax charged on gasoline, aviation fuel, and diesel will be cut in half compared to the regular tax rates. This provides a transition period as the full tax is slowly reintroduced.
key_changes: The federal excise tax on various fuels is suspended until January 31, 2027.
The suspension of the fuel tax is officially backdated to September 8, 2026.
From February 1, 2027, to March 31, 2027, fuel taxes will be set at 50% of their normal rates.
The tax rate on fuel normally charged at $0.10 will be reduced to $0.05 during the transition period.
The tax rate on fuel normally charged at $0.11 will be reduced to $0.055 during the transition period.
The tax rate on fuel normally charged at $0.04 will be reduced to $0.02 during the transition period.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: The Housing Cost Transparency Act requires the National Research Council to provide clear information on the potential costs and decision-making behind changes to national building and housing codes. This helps the public understand how proposed code updates might affect the affordability and complexity of building homes.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary:
The National Research Council is responsible for developing Canada’s national model codes, which cover things like building and fire safety. This bill introduces new rules to make the process of changing these codes more transparent by requiring the Council to publish detailed reports on how proposed changes might impact the cost and construction time of housing.

Additionally, the bill requires the Council to maintain an accessible public registry that tracks these proposals, who suggested them, and how they were decided. Importantly, while the Council provides these models, the bill confirms that provinces, territories, and municipalities keep their sole authority to choose how they adopt and enforce these codes in their own areas.
key_changes: The Council must create a housing cost and impact summary for any proposed code changes that significantly affect building costs or timelines.
These summaries must clearly explain the proposal, its estimated costs for a typical home, and who would be responsible for those costs.
The Council is required to disclose the names and organizational affiliations of the people or groups who requested or sponsored specific code changes.
A public registry must be maintained to track the status of proposals, including information on the committees involved and annual reports on code activity.
For every new edition of a building code, the Council must estimate the combined financial impact on the typical cost of building a home.
The bill explicitly states that these new reporting rules do not take away the power of local or provincial governments to make their own decisions about building codes.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: This bill updates Canadian law to allow the use of psilocybin and psilocin for medical treatments. It also speeds up the government review process for new drugs that are similar to these substances.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary:
This legislation amends the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act and the Food and Drugs Act to officially permit the use of psilocybin and psilocin for medical purposes under existing narcotic control rules. By changing how these substances are classified, the government aims to improve access for patients who may benefit from these specific treatments.

Additionally, the bill changes the approval process for new drugs. It introduces a rule that automatically grants priority review status to submissions involving psilocin, psilocybin, or substances that are chemically similar, ensuring these requests are fast-tracked by the government.
key_changes: Psilocybin and psilocin are now officially categorized as narcotics that can be used for medical treatment.
The legal definition of a restricted drug is updated to exclude psilocybin and psilocin, allowing for their medical use.
Midwives, nurse practitioners, and podiatrists are given authority to handle these specific substances according to their professional regulations.
Requests for priority review of new drugs containing psilocybin or psilocin will now be automatically approved upon submission.
Any substance with a chemical structure similar to psilocybin or psilocin also qualifies for the automatic priority review status.
The purpose of these changes is to expand medical access while still following proper government drug approval procedures.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: This bill removes the federal sales tax from the purchase of used motor vehicles. It aims to make buying a pre-owned car, truck, or motor home more affordable for Canadians.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary:
The Used Car Tax Cut Act changes federal tax rules to classify used motor vehicles as zero-rated supplies. In tax terms, a zero-rated supply means the government charges a tax rate of zero percent on the item, essentially removing the tax burden for the buyer.

This change applies specifically to used vehicles that were previously registered to a different owner under provincial laws. It does not apply to new vehicles that were briefly registered to a dealership only for the purpose of their first official sale.
key_changes: Used motor vehicles are now classified as zero-rated supplies under the Excise Tax Act.
The federal sales tax is removed for qualifying used vehicles designed for highway use.
The rule applies to various types of highway vehicles, including motor homes.
A vehicle must have been previously registered to a different owner to qualify for this tax exemption.
New vehicles registered to a dealer solely for the purpose of their first sale are excluded from this benefit.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/13.tldr: This bill removes a previous law that had banned oil tankers from traveling along the northern coast of British Columbia.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/13.summary:
The Oil Tanker Moratorium Act was a 2019 law that restricted large oil tankers from loading or unloading crude oil at ports along the northern coast of British Columbia. This type of restriction is often called a moratorium, which is a temporary or permanent legal stop on a specific activity.

This new bill cancels the 2019 law entirely. By repealing the act, the government is removing the legal ban that prevented these specific oil shipping activities in that region.
key_changes: The 2019 Oil Tanker Moratorium Act is officially removed from the books.
The legal ban on oil tankers operating in the northern coastal waters of British Columbia is cancelled.
Companies are no longer restricted by this specific act from using ports for oil shipping in that area.
The legislative requirements previously set by the 2019 act are no longer in effect.
This change eliminates the legal framework that governed oil tanker movement in the protected northern zone.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: The Protecting Victims Act creates new laws to address domestic violence and abuse, while strengthening protections and rights for victims throughout the criminal justice system. It introduces specific legal measures to handle coercive control, sexual violence, and harassment more effectively.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary:
This bill updates the Criminal Code to better protect victims of domestic violence and other serious crimes. It defines 'coercive or controlling conduct' toward an intimate partner as a criminal offence and ensures that murder or manslaughter committed under these conditions or in cases of sexual violence or hate-motivated crimes can be treated as first-degree murder or lead to longer prison sentences.

The Act also streamlines court processes to prioritize the safety and dignity of victims. This includes expanding the use of support people or animals in court, making it harder for accused persons to personally cross-examine victims, and improving how evidence of a victim's past sexual history or private therapy records is handled to prevent re-victimization during trials.

Finally, the bill updates various other laws to improve information sharing with victims, modernizes the Youth Criminal Justice Act to better support young victims, and clarifies rules for handling digital evidence like intimate images distributed without consent.
key_changes: A new criminal offence is created for a pattern of coercive or controlling behavior against an intimate partner.
Murder or manslaughter committed against a partner through coercive control or sexual violence may now be classified as first-degree murder.

The definition of criminal harassment is updated to remove the requirement of proving a victim's personal fear, focusing instead on whether the conduct would reasonably cause someone to fear for their safety.
Procedural rules in sexual assault trials are strengthened to protect victim privacy regarding past sexual history and therapeutic records.
Victims of certain offences, such as domestic violence and sexual assault, are now explicitly entitled to use support persons or animals while testifying.
Courts are granted more authority to issue 'no-contact' orders to protect victims from offenders after a conviction.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/13.tldr: The One Canadian Economy Act aims to make it easier to trade goods and move workers between provinces, while creating a faster, centralized process for approving major projects that are deemed to be in the national interest.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/13.summary: Part 1 of the bill works to remove federal barriers to trade and labour mobility within Canada. It establishes that if a product or service meets provincial requirements, it is generally considered to meet federal requirements as well. It also forces federal regulators to recognize professional licenses issued by provinces, making it easier for workers to move and work across the country. The government is granted power to create regulations to further support these goals while maintaining safety and environmental standards. Part 2 focuses on creating an accelerated approval process for large projects considered to be in the national interest. When the government names a project as a national interest project, it can bypass standard individual permits and authorizations. Instead, the Minister issues a single document that covers these required approvals, provided certain conditions are met and consultations with Indigenous peoples and relevant authorities take place.
key_changes: Goods and services that follow provincial rules will now be accepted as meeting comparable federal standards to reduce trade barriers.
Federal bodies must now recognize provincial professional licenses, allowing workers to practice their occupations across provincial borders more easily.
The government can designate specific infrastructure or economic projects as national interest projects to speed up their development.
A single ministerial document can now replace multiple federal permits and approvals for designated national interest projects.
The government must conduct a national security review for foreign investments in any designated national interest project.
The Minister is required to ensure independent annual reviews and public reporting on the progress of all national interest projects.
